content: The Belchertown State School for the Feeble-Minded was established in 1922 in Belchertown, Massachusetts. It was located at 30 State Street and spanned an 876-acre campus, which included ten major buildings designed in the Colonial Revival style by Kendall, Taylor, and Co. Unlike state hospitals, which were intended for individuals with mental illnesses, state schools like Belchertown were institutions for those deemed mentally defective. However, the term school was a misnomer, as these facilities generally did not provide any form of education. For the first 40 years of its operation, Belchertown State School functioned with little external oversight. Over time, it became evident that the residents—some of whom had spent their entire lives in the facility—were subjected to severe mistreatment and abuse by the staff. Author Benjamin Ricci described the conditions as horrific, medieval, and barbaric. Medical professionals at the school often disregarded the mental capacities of the residents. For example, one doctor evaluated a patient solely based on their inability to speak or respond, concluding that the individual was an imbecile or a moron without further assessment. The attendants on the wards were overworked, often responsible for dozens of patients at a time. This led to appalling treatment of the residents. Basic hygiene was neglected, and residents were frequently left half-naked, rolling in their own excrement. Severely physically disabled individuals were confined to their beds all day without any form of stimulation or entertainment. Those unable to feed themselves were force-fed by attendants, often in a rough and injurious manner. When patients needed to be moved, they were handled so roughly that injuries were common. The mistreatment resulted in some residents exhibiting distressing behaviors, such as moaning in the hallways, banging their heads against walls, or smearing feces from their diapers. The facility also suffered from vermin infestations, further exacerbating the inhumane conditions. These issues were partly rooted in the prevailing cultural attitudes of the time, which viewed individuals with disabilities as burdens. In the early 20th century, many families kept disabled individuals at home when possible. However, by the 1920s and 1930s, state governments began creating specialized divisions to manage these populations. In Massachusetts, this responsibility fell to the Department of Mental Retardation. The medical field also began to develop expertise in treating the infirm, which influenced social policies. Despite the deplorable conditions, many parents felt they had no choice but to send their children to such institutions, as there were few alternatives for those with severe disabilities. During the Kennedy administration, awareness of the rights of disabled individuals began to grow, influenced in part by the civil rights movement. In 1966, Massachusetts passed the Mental Health and Retardation Services Act, which aimed to transition from large institutions to community-based care systems. The horrific conditions at Belchertown were exposed in 1971 through a newspaper article titled The Tragedy of Belchertown. Parents filed lawsuits against the school, and when the state Attorney General toured the facility, he described it as a hell hole. This marked the first lawsuit against a state school, paving the way for similar cases in Massachusetts in subsequent years. In 1975, Belchertown faced another lawsuit for denying its residents the right to vote, one of the first disability-related voting rights cases in the United States. In 1977, a case was brought on behalf of a 67-year-old man with severe disabilities and leukemia to determine whether he should be allowed to receive chemotherapy. After years of legal battles and public scrutiny, Belchertown State School was finally closed in 1992. Two years later, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places. In recent years, efforts have been made to repurpose and restore the site. Foley Field was transformed into a baseball diamond for the local Little League team, and the overgrown cemetery, where graves were marked only by numbers, was cleaned and restored to properly memorialize deceased patients by name. In 2001, the town designated the school property as an Economic Opportunity Area for 20 years, offering tax incentives to businesses that established themselves on the site. For further information about Belchertown, Benjamin Ricci's book Crimes Against Humanity: A Historical Perspective provides a detailed account. Ricci, who sent his six-year-old son Bobby to live at the school without knowing the conditions, was involved in the initial 1972 lawsuit. Another book, I Raise My Eyes to Say Yes by Ruth Sienkiewicz-Mercer, offers vivid descriptions of life at Belchertown. Sienkiewicz-Mercer, a former resident of the school during the 1960s and 1970s, recounts her experiences and mentions a young male nurse who worked there during that time. This nurse, John Kerry, later became a junior senator from Massachusetts.
